title: Straight A's, Still Not Ready to Write: What the Science of Writing Says About the 5-Paragraph Essay
author: Randy Barth
summary: Randy Barth responds to a San Francisco Standard story reporting that 1,109 incoming UC Berkeley freshmen had not met the writing requirement, many with near-perfect grades. He argues the gap was built over years of elementary and middle school instruction that gave students a structure to fill in but never taught them to think inside it. The five-paragraph formula is not the problem in itself, but the missing process of planning, deciding what matters and checking the result is. Writing instruction also slipped because it stopped being measured, as California ended its writing tests in 2013 and NAEP has no writing test scheduled through 2033. He cites What Works Clearinghouse guidance and Writing Next, and the strong effects of self-regulated strategy development, and urges daily time for explicit writing instruction in the early grades.
points: Barth reads the Berkeley writing shortfall as the product of years of template-driven instruction, not lazy students or careless teachers.
He argues a template tells students where to put things without teaching the planning and self-checking process behind it.
What is not tested tends not to be taught, and writing assessments have been dropped in California and at the national level.
Explicit strategy instruction, especially self-regulated strategy development, shows the strongest effects in the research he cites.
He urges district leaders to protect daily writing time and teach planning explicitly in elementary and middle grades.
quotes: Their report cards told them they could write, and their first college writing assessment told them something different.
A template tells students where to put things, but it doesn’t teach them the writing process behind it: how to plan, decide what matters, and check whether their writing does what they meant it to.
Bita Nazarian, who runs the San Francisco tutoring nonprofit 826 Valencia, made the point that what doesn’t get tested tends not to get taught.

On best practices in writing instruction, the What Works Clearinghouse recommends at least an hour of writing a day beginning in first grade, with at least half of it spent teaching strategies and skills.
What separates self-regulated strategy development from a template is that students learn the why along with the what.

Explicit planning and self-regulation make the biggest and most lasting difference in the elementary and middle grades, when kids are first figuring out what writing is and whether they’re any good at it.
If we teach kids to think like writers early, the template stops being a ceiling and becomes what it should have been all along, a starting point.
